title: Psychiatric Nursing Overview
body:
## What it is
A map of the psychiatric branch of NP5 (maladaptive patterns of behavior). Use it to find the right note and to see how the pieces fit.
The same map also tells you where the drug notes, substance notes and special therapies live, so you can jump straight to what a question is really testing: a communication choice, a safety decision, a symptom term or a drug point.

## Must-know facts
- Part 1 is the foundation: how the nurse talks, builds a relationship, handles crisis, understands defenses, names symptoms and keeps everyone safe. See [[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Nurse-Patient Relationship Phases]], [[Crisis and Crisis Intervention]], [[Freud's Theory and Defense Mechanisms]], [[Behavioral Management, Restraints and De-escalation]].
- Part 2 covers anxiety, trauma, eating, personality and substance disorders.
- Part 3 covers the big mood and thought disorders and the delirium versus dementia contrast.
- Psych Extra revisits personality clusters, drug classes, developmental disorders, Alzheimer's disease and substances.
- Foundation topics beyond Part 1: [[Mental Health Concepts and History of Psychiatric Care]], [[Therapeutic Use of Self and Johari's Window]], [[Group, Milieu and Family Therapy]], [[Expressive and Insight Therapies]], [[Behavior Modification and Reinforcement]], [[Electroconvulsive Therapy]].
- Communication detail: [[Therapeutic Communication Techniques with Examples]] and [[Non-Therapeutic Communication Blocks with Examples]].
- Drug detail: [[Psychotropic Medication Classes: Which Drug for Which Problem]], [[Antipsychotic Anticholinergic Effects, Clozapine Alert and Client Teaching]], [[Extrapyramidal Symptoms and Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome]], [[Tricyclic and SSRI Antidepressants: Drug Lists and Nursing Care]], [[MAOIs and Other Antidepressants: Tyramine Diet and Special Risks]], [[Lithium Therapy and Toxicity]], [[Antianxiety Drugs: Benzodiazepines and Buspirone]].
- Substance detail: one note per drug family, from [[Alcohol Intoxication and Long-Term Physical Effects]] to [[Opioids: Intoxication, Withdrawal and Naloxone]].
- Childhood and special groups: [[Autism Spectrum Disorder]], [[Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder]], [[Intellectual Disability]].
- Mental health is not just the absence of illness: autonomy, self-esteem, reality orientation, stress management and tolerance of uncertainty are the traits listed as healthy.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Safety of the client and others comes first in every psychiatric question (Maslow: physiologic needs, then safety).
2. Assess before intervening, especially suicide and violence risk.
3. Use the least restrictive effective measure.
4. Then build the relationship and teach.

## How to reason about it
- Stem names a behavior or symptom: first decide whether anyone is in danger now (suicide, violence, command hallucinations, airway after a drug or ECT). Danger beats everything because safety sits right after physiologic needs in Maslow.
- If safety is not at stake, choose the answer that keeps the nurse in a therapeutic role: open, feeling-focused, honest, non-judgmental.
- If the question is about a drug, ask what can kill or harm fastest (airway, fever with rigidity, toxic level, hypertensive crisis, low white cells) and rank that first.
- If two answers both look safe, pick the less restrictive and the more client-centered one.

## How the exam asks about it
Questions blend a communication choice, a safety decision and a drug point. The right answer is usually the one that is safe, calm, honest and focused on the client's feelings rather than on advice or reassurance.

## Related topics
[[Disturbances in Affect and Memory]], [[Disturbances in Perception and Thought]], [[Unusual Speech Patterns]], [[Schizophrenia]], [[Major Depressive Disorder]], [[Bipolar Disorder and Mania]], [[Delirium versus Dementia]], [[Therapeutic Use of Self and Johari's Window]], [[Psychotropic Medication Classes: Which Drug for Which Problem]], [[Electroconvulsive Therapy]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exam weighting between psychiatric and emergency content inside NP5 is UNKNOWN; check the current PRC table of specifications.
- The review handout uses older labels in several places (mental retardation, somatoform, multiple personality, transvestitism). Newer manuals renamed them; learn both names.

title: Therapeutic Communication
body:
## What it is
Purposeful, client-centered communication that helps a person express feelings, solve problems and feel understood. It differs from social talk because it has a goal and focuses on the client, not on the nurse.
Handout goals of therapeutic communication: build the nurse-client relationship, find the client's most important concern right now, learn how the client sees the problem as it unfolded, help the client express emotions, teach the client and family self-care skills, recognize needs, carry out interventions for those needs, and guide the client toward a plan of action that is satisfying and socially acceptable.

## Must-know facts
- Therapeutic techniques: active listening, open-ended questions, reflection (repeating feelings), restating, clarifying, focusing, offering self, giving information, silence, summarizing, and voicing doubt gently when the client holds a false belief.
- Non-therapeutic blocks: false reassurance, giving advice, approving or disapproving, asking "why" (it sounds accusing), changing the subject, defending the staff, stereotyped replies, probing, belittling feelings, and closed questions when feelings are needed.
- Nonverbal behavior counts: sit at the same level, keep open posture, moderate eye contact (respect cultural norms), and match calm tone.
- Silence gives the client time to think; it is a tool, not a failure.
- The full technique list is in [[Therapeutic Communication Techniques with Examples]] (accepting, broad openings, consensual validation, encouraging comparison, encouraging description of perceptions, encouraging expression, exploring, focusing, formulating a plan of action, general leads, giving information, giving recognition, making observations, offering self, placing events in time sequence, presenting reality, reflecting, restating, seeking information, silence, suggesting collaboration, summarizing, translating into feelings, verbalizing the implied, voicing doubt).
- The full list of blocks is in [[Non-Therapeutic Communication Blocks with Examples]]. The classic ones: advising, agreeing, belittling feelings, challenging, defending, disagreeing, approving, literal responses, implying an outside source, interpreting, changing the subject, stereotyped comments, false reassurance, rejecting, asking for an explanation (especially "why"), testing and denial.
- Reflecting hands a question or feeling back to the client ("Do you think you should?"). Restating repeats the main idea in nearly the client's own words. Do not mix them up: reflection targets feeling or the decision, restating targets content.
- Focusing helps when the client jumps from topic to topic; exploring is for going deeper, but respect the client who does not want to explore a subject.
- Presenting reality ("I see no one else in the room") and voicing doubt ("That is hard to believe") are used for false perceptions or beliefs, never to argue.

## What the nurse assesses
- Whether the client's words and body language agree, the pace and content of speech, and readiness to talk.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Ensure safety and privacy first, then open with a broad, non-leading statement.
2. Reflect the feeling before exploring the facts; feelings are the priority in these questions.
3. For a client with hallucinations or delusions, do not argue or agree; state your own perception and acknowledge the client's experience.
4. For a very anxious or confused client, use short, concrete sentences.

## How to reason about it
- Feeling words in the stem point to the answer that names or explores the feeling (reflect, translate into feelings, verbalize the implied). Reason: the client's emotion is the real need; facts and advice come later.
- A "why" question forces the client to defend or justify and sounds like blame. Replace it in your head with "what happened" or "what led up to it".
- A client who says something dramatic or figurative ("I am dead", "a camera is in my head") should get a reply about the feeling, not a literal answer. Reason: literal replies miss the message and may feed the delusion.
- A threat of self-harm is never answered with a change of subject, reassurance or a promise to keep secrets. Ask directly, stay, and act to keep the client safe.
- Silence is chosen when the client is thinking or struggling to find words and the nurse is calm and attentive; it is not chosen for an acutely agitated client who needs a short, clear statement.

## How the exam asks about it
The stem gives a client statement and four replies. Pick the reply that names or explores the feeling in an open way. Eliminate replies that reassure, advise, ask "why", or shut the topic. If the client threatens self-harm, the best reply directly asks about it; never ignore it.

## Memory aid
Invented: "Listen, Reflect, Explore" and avoid the three A's of blocks: Advice, Approval, Argument.

## Related topics
[[Nurse-Patient Relationship Phases]], [[Crisis and Crisis Intervention]], [[Disturbances in Perception and Thought]], [[Major Depressive Disorder]], [[Therapeutic Communication Techniques with Examples]], [[Non-Therapeutic Communication Blocks with Examples]], [[Therapeutic Use of Self and Johari's Window]]

## Check against your textbook
- Your textbook may name additional techniques; learn its list and its example wording.
- The list of technique names and their example sentences differs by book. Learn the names your reviewer uses, since matching a sentence to a technique is a common item.
- Some books place "voicing doubt" as acceptable only when used gently; others warn against it with delusional clients. Check how your reviewer treats it.

title: Nurse-Patient Relationship Phases
body:
## What it is
A professional, goal-directed relationship with defined phases and boundaries. It exists for the client's benefit and ends when goals are met.
The handout describes four phases: pre-orientation, orientation, working and termination. It also calls the relationship goal-directed, focused on the needs of the patient, planned, time-limited and professional.

## Must-know facts
- Common phase model (Peplau-style): orientation, identification, exploitation (working), resolution. Some textbooks use pre-interaction, orientation, working and termination; know both.
- Orientation: introductions, roles, a contract (time, place, purpose, confidentiality limits), building trust, and the client's baseline.
- Working: exploring problems, trying coping skills, promoting insight and behavior change; testing and resistance often appear here.
- Termination: begins at the start; review progress, discuss feelings about ending, and avoid new content.
- Empathy (understanding) differs from sympathy (sharing the feeling); the nurse stays empathic, not sympathetic.
- Boundaries: no gifts, no personal contact outside role, no secrets, no dual relationships. Transference is the client directing feelings about a past person onto the nurse; countertransference is the nurse doing the same.
- Pre-orientation: starts when the nurse is assigned to the client, before any meeting. Major task is developing self-awareness. Tasks are gathering data and planning the first interaction.
- Orientation: begins when nurse and client meet and ends when the client starts to identify problems to work on. Tasks: establishing rapport and trust, assessment, explaining roles and the purpose of meetings, and setting the parameters of later meetings. The major task is a mutually acceptable contract.
- Working: the longest and most productive phase. Limit setting is used here. It has two parts: problem identification (the client names the issues causing trouble) and exploitation (the nurse guides the client to examine feelings and responses and build better coping and a more positive self-image).
- Resistance (ambivalence about self-exploration), transference (client unconsciously moves feelings from a past person onto the nurse) and countertransference (nurse moves her own past feelings onto the client) show up mostly in the working phase.
- Termination (also called resolution): begins when problems are resolved, ends when the relationship ends, and brings anxiety, fear and a sense of loss.
- Basic elements: TRUST. Trust, Rapport, Unconditional positive regard, Setting limits, Therapeutic communication.
- Characteristics to remember: goal-directed, client-centered, planned, time-limited, professional.

## What the nurse assesses
- Trust level, resistance, signs of dependence, and the nurse's own reactions.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Set limits and the contract early; it protects safety and trust.
2. Be consistent, punctual and honest.
3. Handle termination openly; do not make promises to stay in touch.
4. Seek supervision when a client stirs strong personal feelings.

## How to reason about it
- To name the phase, ask what the task is. Introductions, contract and trust: orientation. Client now names problems: working (identification). Looking at feelings and learning coping: working (exploitation). Talking about progress and feelings about ending: termination. Reviewing a chart and own feelings before meeting: pre-orientation.
- Boundary questions are won by the answer that keeps the relationship professional and about the client: no gifts, no secrets, no meeting outside the role, no giving personal phone numbers.
- Strong liking or dislike for a client signals countertransference. Reason: the nurse's reaction is about herself, so the safe step is self-awareness and supervision, not stopping care.
- A client who is late, silent or changes subject when feelings get close may be showing resistance. Accept it calmly; do not punish or confront.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the phase from a described activity, and choose the reply that keeps boundaries. Confidentiality traps: the nurse never promises to keep secrets that threaten safety.

## Related topics
[[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Personality Disorders]], [[Freud's Theory and Defense Mechanisms]], [[Therapeutic Use of Self and Johari's Window]], [[Therapeutic Communication Techniques with Examples]], [[Behavioral Management, Restraints and De-escalation]]

## Check against your textbook
- Which phase names your school uses, and which tasks sit in which phase (books differ).
- The handout phases (pre-orientation, orientation, working, termination) differ from the older Peplau names (orientation, identification, exploitation, resolution). Both appear in books; map them onto each other.
- Which phase "limit setting" belongs to differs by book; the handout puts it in the working phase.

title: Crisis and Crisis Intervention
body:
## What it is
A crisis is a temporary state of disequilibrium when a stressor overwhelms usual coping. It is time-limited, commonly lasting a matter of weeks, and can lead to growth or breakdown.
The handout defines a crisis as a turning point in a person's life that produces an overwhelming emotional response. It is highly individual, usually lasts about 4 to 6 weeks, makes the person passive and submissive, and affects the person's support system. Crisis intervention enters the life situation of an individual, family, group or community to help them mobilize resources and reduce the effect of the stressful event. The goal is the best possible level of functioning.

## Must-know facts
- Types: maturational (developmental, such as adolescence or retirement), situational (job loss, illness, death) and adventitious (disaster, violence, mass events).
- Contributors: a hazardous event, a vulnerable state, a precipitating factor, and lack of coping or support.
- Phases of response run from rising tension, to failed coping, to escalation and disorganization, to resolution or deterioration.
- Crisis intervention is short-term, focused on the present problem, and aims to restore the previous level of functioning. It is not long-term therapy and does not dig into childhood.
- Levels of prevention: primary (prevent), secondary (early crisis intervention), tertiary (rehabilitation after).
- Four phases in the handout: denial (first reaction); increased tension (the person sees the crisis but keeps doing daily activities); disorganization (preoccupied, unable to do daily activities); attempts to reorganize (old coping methods are called up).
- Two intervention styles: authoritative (assess health status, give information, give feedback about behavior, suggest courses of action) and facilitative (empathy, helping the client name and discuss feelings, acting as a sounding board, affirming self-worth). Details: [[Crisis Types, Phases and Intervention Styles]].
- The nurse's primary role is active and directive.
- Rape is a social crisis with its own syndrome and care steps: [[Rape, Rape Trauma Syndrome and Survivor Care]].

## What the nurse assesses
- The event and its meaning, perceived threat, available support, coping skills tried, and suicide or violence risk.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Assess safety, including suicidal thoughts, first.
2. Be directive, calm and present; the client may not think clearly.
3. Help the client state the problem, explore options and choose one.
4. Mobilize family and community support and link to follow-up.
5. Evaluate whether functioning returned.

## How to reason about it
- Ask what the client can still do. Still doing daily tasks: increased tension, so help problem-solving. Cannot do daily tasks: disorganization, so the nurse takes a more directive role (simple choices, concrete steps) because the client cannot decide well.
- The first action is safety (suicide, violence), because a person in crisis may think of self-harm. Then focus on the here and now. Digging into childhood is wrong in a crisis; time is short and the client is overwhelmed.
- Choose "mobilize the support system and past coping" over "wait for the client to find a solution".

## How the exam asks about it
A grieving or newly diagnosed client shows disorganization; the answer is short-term, here-and-now, active nursing support, not insight therapy. Distinguish crisis types from stems.

## Memory aid
Invented: "Safe, Name it, Options, Support."

## Related topics
[[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorders]], [[Disaster Nursing Basic Concepts|Disaster Nursing]], [[Crisis Types, Phases and Intervention Styles]], [[Rape, Rape Trauma Syndrome and Survivor Care]], [[Acute Stress Disorder versus Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder]]

## Check against your textbook
- Typical duration and the exact phase model your textbook uses (verify). Philippine crisis lines and program details: verify local policy.
- The old note says "commonly lasting a matter of weeks"; the handout states 4 to 6 weeks. Phase models differ among books (some use four phases from Caplan, some three).
- The maturational versus situational versus adventitious wording is used in older books; the handout calls the third type social.

title: Freud's Theory and Defense Mechanisms
body:
## What it is
Freud described personality as three structures and development in psychosexual stages. Defense mechanisms are unconscious ways the ego reduces anxiety.
Handout view of the structures: the id seeks instant gratification, acts impulsively and ignores rules. The superego holds values and parental and social expectations, so it opposes the id. The ego mediates between them; it represents mature, adaptive behavior that lets a person function in the world.

## Must-know facts
- Structures: id (instinct, pleasure, immediate), ego (reality, mediator), superego (conscience, ideals).
- Levels of mind: conscious, preconscious, unconscious.
- Psychosexual stages: oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital.
- Common defenses: repression (pushing thoughts out of awareness), suppression (conscious pushing away), denial, projection (blaming others for own feelings), displacement (shifting feelings to a safer target), rationalization (logical excuses), reaction formation (acting opposite to true feeling), regression (return to earlier behavior), identification, introjection, sublimation (channeling urges into acceptable activity, considered healthy), undoing, compensation, intellectualization, isolation of affect, splitting, conversion and dissociation.
- Immature defenses often seen in personality and psychotic disorders; sublimation, humor and altruism are mature.
- Levels of awareness: conscious (what you are aware of now), preconscious (not in awareness now but recalled with effort, for example remembering something from childhood), unconscious (the largest part; it holds motives and most defense mechanisms and material that can never be recalled directly).
- Repression: unconscious forgetting of painful thoughts (no memory of a mugging that happened yesterday). Suppression: conscious forgetting (trying to forget past money problems).
- Rationalization: excuses one's behavior to avoid responsibility, conflict or loss of self-respect (blames a failing grade on a mean teacher).
- Reaction formation: acts opposite to what one feels (a woman who never wanted children becomes a super-mom; despising the boss but praising the boss to everyone).
- Regression: moves back to an earlier stage to feel safe (a five-year-old asks for a bottle when the baby brother is fed).
- Displacement: vents intense feelings on a less threatening person (angry at the boss, yells at the spouse).
- Compensation: overachieves in one area to offset a real or imagined weakness in another (a nurse with low self-esteem works double shifts so the supervisor will like her).
- Conversion: an emotional conflict becomes a physical symptom, usually in movement or senses (a teenager forbidden to watch x-rated movies develops blindness and is unconcerned).
- Denial: refuses to admit an unbearable reality (a diabetic eating candy, waiting three days with severe abdominal pain).

## What the nurse assesses
- Behavior that reduces anxiety but distorts reality, and how rigidly it is used.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Do not confront or strip a defense away in an acutely anxious client; it is protection.
2. Address the underlying anxiety and teach healthier coping.
3. Set limits on harmful behavior (such as acting out) while accepting the person.

## How to reason about it
- Ask two questions. Was the forgetting conscious or not (repression versus suppression)? Did the feeling go to a safer target (displacement), come back at the person as a body symptom (conversion), or get turned into its opposite (reaction formation)?
- Reason about the nurse's response: defenses lower anxiety, so they are not attacked in a client who is acutely anxious. The nurse treats the anxiety first, then helps build healthier coping.
- Compensation and sublimation are generally healthy or neutral; denial, projection, regression and conversion are the ones linked to illness.

## How the exam asks about it
A short vignette is given; name the defense. Look-alikes: repression vs suppression (unconscious vs conscious), displacement vs projection, denial vs rationalization.

## Memory aid
Invented: projection = "it's YOU"; displacement = "kick the dog"; reaction formation = "protests too much".

## Related topics
[[Anxiety and Anxiety Disorders]], [[Phobic and Somatic Symptom Disorders]], [[Personality Disorders]], [[Expressive and Insight Therapies]], [[Dissociative Disorders and Grounding Care]], [[Somatoform Disorders: Gains, Theories and Management]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact stage ages, and which defenses your textbook classes as mature, neurotic or immature.
- The handout treats unconscious material as "can never be recalled"; most books say it can surface through dreams, free association or therapy. Learn the answer your reviewer expects.
- Some books list conversion and dissociation as separate defenses; others fold them into the disorders they cause.

title: Disturbances in Affect and Memory
body:
## What it is
Vocabulary for describing mental status findings. Mood is the sustained inner emotion; affect is the outward expression seen by others.

## Must-know facts
Affect:
- Flat: almost no expression. Blunted: reduced. Constricted: narrowed range. Labile: swings rapidly. Inappropriate (incongruent): does not match the content. Broad: normal range.
- Euphoria: intense elation. Elation: joy with confidence. Ambivalence: opposite feelings together. Apathy: lack of interest. Anhedonia: no pleasure from usual activities. Dysphoria: unpleasant mood. Anxiety, fear and depersonalization also belong in this group.

Memory:
- Amnesia: loss of memory (anterograde forward, retrograde backward).
- Confabulation: filling gaps with made-up details, without intent to lie, typical in alcohol-related memory disorders.
- Paramnesia includes deja vu (feeling already seen) and jamais vu (familiar feels new).
- Hypermnesia: excessive recall. Dissociative amnesia follows stress; organic amnesia follows brain injury or illness.
- Handout affect terms: inappropriate affect (the emotion does not fit the situation), blunted affect (severe reduction), flat affect (almost none), apathy (indifference toward people, activities and events), ambivalence (two opposing feelings at once).
- Depersonalization: feeling detached from oneself; the client may state his name correctly but feel the body belongs to someone else or that the spirit has left the body. Derealization: strangeness toward the environment; objects seem larger, smaller or unfamiliar, the world looks changed or gray and dull. Mnemonic: depersonalization is about "me", derealization is about "it" (the world).
- Motor disturbances: echopraxia (pathologic imitation of another person's movements or posture) and waxy flexibility (holding an awkward position for long periods without discomfort), both catatonic signs.
- Confabulation: filling a memory gap with a detailed fantasy that the person believes, and its purpose is to protect self-esteem. Example: a resident insists she played cards with the husband of another resident who died years before she met them. Amnesia: inability to recall past events.

## What the nurse assesses
- Mental status exam: appearance, behavior, speech, mood and affect, thought, perception, cognition, insight and judgment.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Describe what you see in objective words, not labels.
2. Rule out physical causes for sudden memory change.
3. Orient gently and ensure safety when memory is impaired.

## How to reason about it
- Find the clue word in the stem. "Cannot remember, then makes up a story" is confabulation (protects self-esteem), not lying. "Feels body belongs to someone else" is depersonalization. "Everything looks gray and unreal" is derealization. "Shows no facial reaction at all" is flat; "a little reaction" is blunted.
- For a client with memory gaps, safety and orientation come before testing memory. Reason: arguing with or quizzing a confabulating client harms self-esteem and gains nothing.
- Sudden new confusion or memory loss is a medical problem until proven otherwise (low oxygen, infection, glucose, drugs).

## How the exam asks about it
Match the term to the example. Traps: flat vs blunted; confabulation vs lying; mood vs affect.

## Related topics
[[Major Depressive Disorder]], [[Schizophrenia]], [[Alcohol Use Disorder]], [[Delirium versus Dementia]], [[Unusual Speech Patterns]], [[Dissociative Disorders and Grounding Care]], [[Schizophrenia]]

## Check against your textbook
- Definitions of paramnesia subtypes differ by source.
- Handout lists ambivalence as an affect disturbance; some books place it with thought or with schizophrenia's signs. Depersonalization is both a symptom and a disorder, so read the stem for which is asked.

title: Disturbances in Perception and Thought
body:
## What it is
Perception disturbances are abnormal sensory experiences; thought disturbances are abnormal content (what is thought) or process (how thoughts flow).

## Must-know facts
Perception:
- Hallucination: sensory experience with no external stimulus (auditory most common in schizophrenia; visual suggests delirium or substance effects; tactile suggests withdrawal or substance use; olfactory or gustatory may suggest seizure or brain disease).
- Illusion: misreading a real stimulus. Depersonalization: feeling unreal in oneself. Derealization: surroundings feel unreal. Hypnagogic and hypnopompic: at sleep onset or waking.

Thought content:
- Delusion: fixed false belief resistant to proof. Types: persecutory, grandiose, somatic, religious, jealous, reference, nihilistic.
- Ideas of reference, thought broadcasting, insertion and withdrawal, obsession, compulsion, phobia, magical thinking, overvalued idea, poverty of content.

Thought process:
- Loose associations, flight of ideas, tangentiality, circumstantiality, blocking, perseveration, neologism, concrete thinking, thought poverty.
- Handout definitions: a delusion is a false belief inconsistent with the person's knowledge and culture (for example claiming to be engaged to a movie star or the child of a national leader). A hallucination is a false sensory perception, a perceptual experience that does not really exist (for example hearing a voice that commands harm to another person).
- Thought-process terms with handout examples: circumstantial thinking (too many unnecessary details, but finally reaches the point), tangential thinking (too many details and never gets to the point), word salad (jumbled disconnected words), verbigeration (stereotyped repetition of words or phrases), perseveration (keeps returning to one idea or repeats a word despite attempts to change the topic), echolalia (repeats what the nurse says), flight of ideas (a rush of fragmented or unrelated ideas), loose associations (jumps from idea to idea with little connection), neologism (invented word).
- More detail on delusion types, thought broadcasting, insertion and blocking is in [[Delusion Types and Thought Disturbances in Schizophrenia]].

## What the nurse assesses
- Content of voices (especially commands to harm self or others), distress, and how much the client acts on them.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Ask about command hallucinations; if present, safety is the priority.
2. Do not argue with or confirm a delusion; present reality calmly and focus on feelings.
3. Reduce stimulation; stay with a frightened client.
4. Give antipsychotics as ordered and watch effects.

## How to reason about it
- Separate form from content. Content is what the person believes (delusion, obsession). Form is how thoughts flow (tangential, flight of ideas). Perception is what the senses report (hallucination, illusion).
- Circumstantial versus tangential: both wander, only circumstantial returns. Perseveration versus verbigeration: perseveration sticks to a topic or idea despite redirection; verbigeration is empty repeated words.
- Nursing reasoning: a voice that gives commands is a safety question first (what does it say, will you obey it). Disagreeing with a delusion (challenging) makes the client defend it. Agreeing confirms it. Present reality calmly, state what you see, and talk about the feeling the belief produces.
- Fear is the common ground: a frightened client needs a calm nurse, low stimulation and short sentences.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the term from an example, or choose the reply to a client who says people are following them: acknowledge fear, state you see no evidence, and offer safety.

## Memory aid
Invented: hallucination = sees without a screen; illusion = misreads the screen.

## Related topics
[[Schizophrenia]], [[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Unusual Speech Patterns]], [[Typical and Atypical Antipsychotics]], [[Delusion Types and Thought Disturbances in Schizophrenia]], [[Non-Therapeutic Communication Blocks with Examples]], [[Disturbances in Affect and Memory]]

## Check against your textbook
- Fine definitions (for example circumstantiality vs tangentiality) vary by text.
- Some books class ideas of reference as delusions, others as milder ideas short of a delusion. Verify.

title: Unusual Speech Patterns
body:
## What it is
Abnormal form or amount of speech that points to disordered thinking, mood episodes or brain disease.

## Must-know facts
- Echolalia: repeating what another says. Palilalia: repeating own words. Verbigeration: meaningless repetition of words or phrases.
- Clang association: choosing words by sound (rhyming), often in mania.
- Word salad: jumbled words with no meaning. Neologism: invented word. Mutism: not speaking. Pressured speech: rapid, hard to interrupt, typical of mania. Poverty of speech: very little speech.
- Loose associations and flight of ideas are process disturbances that show up in speech.
- Aphasia is a language deficit from brain injury and is not a psychiatric symptom, but may appear in questions as a contrast.
- Echopraxia is imitation of movements, listed beside echolalia in catatonia.
- Handout examples to anchor the terms. Word salad: "corn, potatoes, jump up, play games, grass, cupboard." Verbigeration: "I want to go home, go home, go home." Neologism: "I'm afraid of grittiz." Echolalia: nurse asks "How are you feeling?" and client says "How are you feeling?" Flight of ideas: "The sun is shining. Where is my sun? I love Lucy. Let us play ball." Loose associations: one thought slides to another with no visible link (candy bar to yen to the Swiss to holes).
- Clang associations (in schizophrenia notes of the handout): words chosen by sound or rhyme, such as "pill, hill, Jill, kill."
- Circumstantial and tangential speech are about excess detail; circumstantial reaches the point, tangential does not.
- Thought blocking: stopping abruptly in the middle of a sentence and sometimes unable to continue. Alogia: poverty of content, speech that has little real meaning (a vague answer such as "I do not know... it's hard to tell").

## What the nurse assesses
- Rate, volume, fluency and logic, and whether speech makes sense in context.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Stay calm; use short, clear statements.
2. Do not pretend to understand; say what you did understand and ask again.
3. Check for medical causes if speech changes suddenly (stroke, delirium).

## How to reason about it
- Judge by what the listener can follow. Cannot follow at all: word salad. Can follow, but the speaker takes a long road: circumstantial. Rapid, pressured and topic changes by link of meaning: flight of ideas (mania). Topic changes by sound: clang. Silence mid-sentence: blocking.
- Nursing action follows the same logic: when speech is disorganized, use short, concrete questions, one at a time. Do not pretend to understand and do not correct the speech.
- A new speech change in an older person is a medical alert (stroke, delirium), not just a psychiatric symptom.

## How the exam asks about it
Name the term from an example. Memorize pairs: echolalia (copies others), clang (rhymes), word salad (jumble), neologism (new word).

## Related topics

title: Behavioral Management, Restraints and De-escalation
body:
## What it is
Methods to keep clients and staff safe when behavior becomes aggressive or self-harming. The principle is the least restrictive, effective measure, used for the shortest time.

## Must-know facts
- Escalation order: verbal de-escalation and environment changes first; then voluntary time-out or medication as ordered; then seclusion or physical restraint only when there is imminent danger and less restrictive options fail.
- Restraints and seclusion require a prescriber order and face-to-face evaluation within a short time after starting; renewal is time-limited. Exact time limits depend on age and policy: verify.
- Restraints are never for convenience, punishment or staff shortage.
- Continuous or frequent observation, circulation and skin checks, hydration, toileting, comfort and dignity are required; document reason, alternatives tried, client response and release criteria.
- Behavior therapy tools: positive reinforcement, token economy, limit setting, extinction, time-out, modeling.
- Behavior modification (see [[Behavior Modification and Reinforcement]]) strengthens a wanted behavior with reinforcement. Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant after the behavior. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant right after it. Both make the behavior more likely; neither is punishment.
- Milieu therapy uses a deliberately controlled environment so the setting itself supports change; see [[Group, Milieu and Family Therapy]].
- The least restrictive effective measure is the guiding rule in every restraint or seclusion question.

## What the nurse assesses
- Triggers, early warning signs (pacing, clenched fists, loud voice, threats), intoxication, pain, delirium or unmet needs, and weapons risk.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Protect safety and call for help early; keep a team.
2. Approach calmly, give space, speak low and slow, offer choices, and set clear, short limits.
3. Remove the audience and reduce stimulation.
4. If restraint is unavoidable, use trained staff, maintain airway and breathing, and monitor continuously.
5. Debrief the client and staff afterward.

## How to reason about it
- Walk the ladder from the bottom: space and calm voice, then reduce stimulation, then a voluntary time-out, then medication as ordered, and only then seclusion or restraint if there is immediate danger. Reason: each step takes away more freedom, so it is justified only when the one before cannot keep people safe.
- While restrained, the client is a physiologic priority: airway, breathing, circulation, hydration, toileting, skin and circulation of limbs. Reason: a restrained, agitated or sedated person can aspirate, overheat or injure nerves, and cannot call for help.
- After the event the order is client safe, then debrief the client, then staff, then document. Never leave "convenience" or "punishment" as the reason.
- If the stem says the client is intoxicated, delirious or in pain, treat that cause: the aggression may be a symptom.

## How the exam asks about it
Choose the least restrictive first step. Trap: jumping to restraint or injection before verbal de-escalation, or leaving a restrained client unobserved. Another trap: arguing with a client who is escalating.

## Memory aid
Invented: "Talk, Space, Medicine, Hold."

## Related topics
[[Crisis and Crisis Intervention]], [[Typical and Atypical Antipsychotics]], [[Schizophrenia]], [[Alcohol Use Disorder]], [[Behavior Modification and Reinforcement]], [[Group, Milieu and Family Therapy]], [[Antipsychotic Anticholinergic Effects, Clozapine Alert and Client Teaching]]

## Check against your textbook
- Order and duration rules; Philippine mental health law and facility policy: verify local policy.
- Time limits for orders, face-to-face evaluation and renewal come from law and facility policy, not from this handout.

title: Anxiety and Anxiety Disorders
body:
## What it is
Anxiety is a vague, uneasy feeling of dread from an unknown or unrecognized threat; fear is a response to a known threat. Anxiety disorders are anxiety that is excessive, persistent and disabling.

## Must-know facts
- Levels: mild (alert, learning improves), moderate (narrowed attention, selective inattention, can still follow direction), severe (perception greatly narrowed, focus on scattered details, cannot learn), panic (loss of control, disorganized, terror, possible harm).
- Disorders in this family: generalized anxiety disorder (chronic worry about many things, for months), panic disorder (sudden attacks of intense fear with physical symptoms, usually peaking within minutes), agoraphobia, social anxiety, specific phobia, separation anxiety. OCD and trauma disorders are now grouped separately: see [[Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders]] and [[Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorders]].
- Physical signs: tachycardia, rapid breathing, sweating, tremor, dry mouth, nausea, dizziness. Rule out medical causes (thyroid, cardiac, caffeine, drug effects).
- Handout level details: mild anxiety widens the perceptual field and sharpens learning and problem solving; moderate narrows the field to the immediate task and the person can learn or solve problems only with help; severe brings dread or terror, scattered details, tachycardia, sweating and chest pain (these clients often go to the emergency room fearing a heart attack); panic brings loss of rational thought, possible delusions or hallucinations, immobility or muteness, or bolting and running aimlessly with risk of injury.
- Type-by-type criteria: [[Panic Disorder, Agoraphobia, Social Phobia and Generalized Anxiety Disorder]] and [[Acute Stress Disorder versus Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder]].
- Handout principles of care: stay calm, give medication as ordered, listen to the concern, reduce environmental stimuli. Priority diagnoses: anxiety and ineffective individual coping.

## What the nurse assesses
- Anxiety level, triggers, physical symptoms, coping, safety, substance use.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Stay with the client; a calm presence is first, especially in panic. Maslow: safety.
2. Reduce stimulation, use short, simple directions, and move to a quiet place.
3. Do not touch without permission in severe anxiety.
4. Once calmer, explore triggers and teach breathing, relaxation and grounding.
5. Teach only when anxiety is mild; learning fails at severe levels.

## Medications and treatments (general terms)
- Benzodiazepines act quickly but risk dependence and sedation; use short term. Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs) are common first-line for long-term control. Buspirone is non-sedating and slow acting. Beta-blockers can reduce performance anxiety. Cognitive behavioral therapy and relaxation are core.

## Client and family teaching
- Avoid caffeine and alcohol, do not stop medication suddenly, practice relaxation daily, and report worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm.

## How to reason about it
- Chest pain, sweating and a racing pulse in an anxious client are first treated as possibly cardiac. Reason: a physical emergency outranks a psychological label, so assess before assuming anxiety.
- The nurse's calm presence is the first intervention at every level. As the level rises, the nurse does less asking and teaching and more staying, simplifying and protecting.
- Learning is possible only at mild or low moderate levels. A teaching answer is wrong for severe or panic anxiety.
- Medication follows safety: anxiolytics relieve symptoms but do not treat the cause, so coping skills are still taught afterward.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the level from behaviors, then choose an action that fits the level. Trap: teaching or asking for decisions in severe or panic anxiety.

## Memory aid
Invented: mild = "I notice", moderate = "I narrow", severe = "I scatter", panic = "I flee".

## Related topics
[[Freud's Theory and Defense Mechanisms]], [[Phobic and Somatic Symptom Disorders]], [[Antidepressants and Mood Stabilizers]], [[Panic Disorder, Agoraphobia, Social Phobia and Generalized Anxiety Disorder]], [[Anxiolytic Drugs and Cognitive-Behavioral Techniques for Anxiety]], [[Antianxiety Drugs: Benzodiazepines and Buspirone]]

## Check against your textbook
- Drug onset and duration details; the exact diagnostic grouping your textbook uses (older books keep OCD and PTSD under anxiety).
- Handout says panic attacks last 15 to 30 minutes; many books say they peak within about 10 minutes. Handout names SSRIs as safest drug during a panic attack, which is odd because SSRIs act slowly; benzodiazepines are the rapid option. Verify both.
